en: Jātaka:
The Section of Sevens, Chapter on the Hen-Fowl (Kukkuvagga)
9. The Kapi Jātaka:
“Where an enemy dwells, there a wise person should not live.”
For one night or two nights,
the person of light mind dwells in suffering among enemies.
Indeed, in every direction, for the one of fickle mind—
By following the lead of its master,
for the sake of a single monkey,
ruin was brought upon the entire herd.
Like a fool who fancies himself wise,
acting as the leader of the herd,
he falls under the sway of his own mind.
It would be as if this monkey were saying:
"It is not right for a strong fool to be the protector of the herd."
He becomes a source of harm to his kinsmen,
like a cheta bird to other birds;
whereas the wise man is indeed good and strong.
He is the protector of his herd;
he becomes a benefactor to his kinsmen,
just as Vāsava is to the Thirty-three gods.
But he who perceives in himself both virtue and wisdom, and learning—
such a one practices for the welfare of both.
Both for oneself and for another.
Therefore, one should weigh oneself, as one would weigh one's own virtue, wisdom, and learning.
“A wise person should either lead a group or wander alone.
Thus ends the ninth Jātaka, the Kapi-jātaka.
